passage:
Karthik: bro everyone's going to the quarry tonight. jumping off the ledge 🤩
Baljeet: the flooded one? isn't it deep and dark
Karthik: that's the point lol. Arjun did it last week
Karthik: if I don't go they'll call me scared again
Baljeet: ok but it's midnight and nobody can see the rocks
Karthik: you sound like my mom
Baljeet: fine. but you're typing like 100 words a min. you ok?
Karthik: I'm just hyped
Karthik: also kinda annoyed they laughed at me at practice
Baljeet: so this is about that?
Karthik: ...maybe
Baljeet: what if you say you'll come in the daytime on Sunday. see it properly
Karthik: they'll say I'm chickening out
Baljeet: let them. we'll go together in daylight
Karthik: ok. yeah. sleeping instead 😴

qa.q: Where was everyone planning to go that night?
qa.a: To the flooded quarry to jump off the ledge.

qa.q: What feeling does Karthik admit is really pushing the plan to go?
qa.a: Karthik is annoyed that the others laughed at practice and wants to prove not being scared, so hurt pride and excitement are driving the choice.

qa.q: What worked in how Baljeet helped Karthik decide?
qa.a: Baljeet noticed Karthik's rush, asked about the real feeling behind it, and offered a calmer daytime option together instead of just saying no.

qa.q: How might the group see Karthik if he skips tonight?
qa.a: Some may tease Karthik for chickening out, but that teasing is exactly the pressure Baljeet helps Karthik see past.

grounding: Shows a teen, with a friend's help, slowing down a risky choice driven by excitement, hurt pride and peer pressure.

passage: At the Dussehra mela in their kasba, the older boys crowded around Bhupen's uncle's motorbike. "Divyansh, take a round," one said, tossing him the keys. "Just to the canal and back." Divyansh's heart pounded. He was sixteen and had no licence, and he'd only ever ridden it slowly in the courtyard. The boys started chanting his name. His hand closed on the keys. Then Bhupen caught his eye and gave a tiny shake of the head. Divyansh said, "Wait, let me get a chai first," and walked to the stall, away from the noise. He sipped, watched the crowded road and the tractor lights. By the time he came back, his hands were steady. He handed the keys back. "Not today." A couple of boys booed. He shrugged and went to the giant wheel.

qa.q: Where did the boys want Divyansh to ride the motorbike to?
qa.a: To the canal and back.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when the boys started chanting his name?
qa.a: He was excited and under intense pressure, with a pounding heart, and part of him wanted to prove himself.

qa.q: Why was stepping away for chai a smart move?
qa.a: It gave him a few minutes away from the chanting to calm down and see the crowded road clearly before deciding.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see the situation?
qa.a: He seems worried, since it is his uncle's bike and the road is crowded, and his small head shake signals that he hopes Divyansh will say no.

grounding: Shows a teen cooling down in a heated moment of peer pressure before making a safer choice.

passage: In her bedroom in Dublin, Dalia got a text from Liam: "You told everyone about my parents?? Thanks a lot." She hadn't. Her face went hot. Her thumbs flew across the screen: "Are you serious?? I'd NEVER do that, you're paranoid and honestly exhausting." Her finger hovered over send. She remembered last spring, when she'd sent something similar to a friend and they hadn't spoken for months. She put the phone face down on the bed, went downstairs and made toast she didn't really want. She texted her cousin a rant instead. Twenty minutes later, she deleted her draft and wrote: "I didn't tell anyone. I'm upset you'd think that. Can we talk tomorrow?" Liam replied the next morning: "Sorry. Someone else said it was you."

qa.q: What did Liam accuse Dalia of in his text?
qa.a: He accused her of telling everyone about his parents.

qa.q: What made Dalia pause before sending her first reply?
qa.a: She remembered how a similar angry message last spring cost her a friendship for months.

qa.q: What could Dalia try again the next time she feels that heat?
qa.a: Put the phone away and do something ordinary until the anger settles, then write a calm message that states her feelings.

qa.q: How might things have gone for Liam if Dalia had sent the first draft?
qa.a: He would have felt attacked while already upset about his parents, and the misunderstanding could have become a long falling-out.

grounding: Shows a teen noticing her emotional heat and delaying a reply to make a cooler, wiser choice.

passage: At the district basketball match in the club gym, a girl from the other team elbowed Jahnavi hard in the ribs under the basket. The referee missed it. Jahnavi's face went hot, and she spun round, ready to shove back. Gautam, her team's assistant coach, was shouting something from the bench, but she couldn't hear it over the crowd. Then she saw the scoreboard: two fouls already against her name. One more and she'd sit out the final quarter. She unclenched her fists, turned her back, and jogged to her position, breathing out hard. At the timeout, Gautam said, 'I thought you'd swing.' 'I almost did,' she said, still shaking. 'Then I did the maths.'

qa.q: How many fouls did Jahnavi already have?
qa.a: Two fouls.

qa.q: What does 'I almost did' show about Jahnavi's state in that moment?
qa.a: She was flooded with anger and close to shoving back, and only just caught herself.

qa.q: What helped Jahnavi cool her choice, and how could she practise it?
qa.a: Looking at the scoreboard gave her a reason to pause; she could practise a set cue, like one breath and a glance, for heated moments.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt watching from the bench?
qa.a: Worried she would retaliate, then relieved and proud when she held back.

grounding: Shows a teenager catching herself in a moment of hot anger and choosing with a cooler head.

passage:
Dear Sudha Aunty,
You told me to write when something happened that I didn't want to tell Ammi yet, so here it is. On Saturday some boys from my building were daring each other to race scooters down the flyover ramp without helmets. They'd filmed two already and everyone was screaming. It was my turn. My heart was banging and I actually had my hand on the handle. Then I remembered what you said about deciding things 'before the crowd arrives.' I'd already decided, weeks ago: no dares on roads. So I said, 'Not doing it. I'll film.' They called me scared. I was, a bit. But I'd rather be scared on the pavement. I'll tell Ammi this weekend.
Tanvir

qa.q: What had Tanvir decided weeks ago?
qa.a: No dares on roads.

qa.q: What do Tanvir's banging heart and hand on the handle suggest Tanvir was feeling?
qa.a: Tanvir was caught up in the excitement and pressure and was close to going along with it.

qa.q: What lesson from this could help Tanvir in future heated moments?
qa.a: Deciding limits calmly in advance, so Tanvir has a ready answer when the crowd and excitement hit.

qa.q: How might Sudha Aunty feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Relieved Tanvir was safe, proud that her advice helped, and glad Tanvir plans to tell Ammi. 🙏

grounding: Illustrates a teenager resisting a risky dare under peer pressure by relying on a decision made in a calm moment.

passage: Vidya, you want the scooter story for your project? Fine. I'm Jagdish, I was seventeen. It was midnight after a wedding, and my friends wanted to ride three on one scooter, no helmets, to the highway dhaba. Everyone was loud, laughing, daring me. I had the keys. My heart was going fast and I wanted to say yes so badly. Then I remembered what our PE sir said: when you're hot, wait ten minutes before you decide. So I said I needed the bathroom and stood there, counting. When I came back, I said no. They called me boring. Two of them walked home with me anyway.

qa.q: How many friends wanted to ride on one scooter?
qa.a: Three on one scooter.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when holding the keys?
qa.a: Jagdish felt excited, pressured and tempted, with a racing heart.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Taking ten minutes to cool down, because it let calmer thinking take over before deciding.

qa.q: How might the two friends who walked home with Jagdish have felt?
qa.a: Maybe relieved, glad someone said no so they didn't have to.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning to delay a risky decision made under excitement and peer pressure.

passage: I'm Kiran, Jeevan's teammate. In Saturday's match, a boy from the other side slid in hard and caught Jeevan's ankle on purpose. Jeevan, sixteen, jumped up, fists clenched, face red, and took two steps towards him. Everyone froze. Then he stopped, turned round, and walked to the touchline. He stood there with his hands on his head, breathing hard. After a minute he came back and told the referee, calmly, what had happened. The boy got a yellow card. I don't know what went on in his head in those seconds, but it was the calmest I've seen him.

qa.q: What did the boy from the other side do?
qa.a: He slid in hard and caught Jeevan's ankle on purpose.

qa.q: What might Jeevan have felt when he took two steps towards the boy?
qa.a: He was probably furious and hurt, wanting to hit back.

qa.q: What did Jeevan do that helped him choose well?
qa.a: He walked away to the touchline to cool down before going to the referee.

qa.q: How does Kiran see Jeevan's reaction?
qa.a: Kiran was surprised by how calm he became, though Kiran can't know what he was thinking.

grounding: Shows a teenager stopping himself from acting on intense anger and choosing a cooler response, seen by a teammate.

passage: Friday night: Manjula, fifteen, found out her friend Sunaina had told others about her crush. Furious, she typed a long message full of insults, finger over send. Instead she saved it as a draft and went to sleep, still angry. Saturday: she reread it. Some of it made her wince. She deleted half. Sunday: she met Sunaina in person. "I felt betrayed when you told everyone." Sunaina's face fell. "I thought it was a joke. I'm really sorry." Manjula was glad she hadn't sent the draft. The words she'd almost said would have been impossible to take back.

qa.q: What did Manjula do with the angry message on Friday night?
qa.a: She saved it as a draft and went to sleep.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when she reread the message on Saturday?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed at how harsh it was.

qa.q: What helped Manjula make a better choice?
qa.a: Waiting until she was calm and then speaking in person about how she felt.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt when Manjula spoke calmly?
qa.a: Guilty and sorry, and more able to apologise than if she'd been attacked.

grounding: Shows a teenager over a weekend learning to hold back a choice made in anger and respond more coolly.

passage: Rafiq Chacha stirred his tea slowly. "Kamal, when I was sixteen, my friends and I had new bikes. One evening on the highway, Irshad shouted, 'Race to the toll booth! Loser buys tea!' Everyone revved. My heart was pounding, my blood was hot, and I wanted to win so badly. Then I saw the truck in front and remembered my Abba saying, 'When you're excited, count to five before you act.' I counted. One, two, three... and I let them go. I rode slowly to the toll booth. Irshad got there first, and he had skidded and scraped his whole leg. He could have been worse. I paid for the tea anyway." Kamal grinned. "You lost, then." "I lost the race," Chacha said. "Nothing else."

qa.q: Where did Irshad want to race to?
qa.a: To the toll booth.

qa.q: How did young Rafiq feel when Irshad shouted "Race"?
qa.a: He felt excited and pumped up, heart pounding and wanting badly to win.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Rafiq's story?
qa.a: Seeing the truck and remembering his father's rule to count to five before acting when excited.

qa.q: How might Irshad have felt after scraping his leg?
qa.a: He was probably shaken and in pain, and may have regretted starting the race.

grounding: An uncle remembers counting to five to calm down during a peer-pressured bike race as a teenager.

passage: It was 11 p.m., the night before the chemistry exam, and Sabina's phone was at nine percent. Then she saw the group chat: Nandini had posted a photo from the party Sabina wasn't invited to. Her face went hot. She typed fast: "Wow, thanks for inviting me, fake friends. Hope you had fun." Her thumb hovered over send. The screen dimmed. She called Nandini instead, but Nandini didn't answer. Sabina put the phone down, breathing hard. She reread her message. In the morning, would she still mean it? She deleted it and wrote in her notebook instead: "Ask N tomorrow, calmly." She plugged in her phone and opened the chemistry book, though her hands were still trembling.

qa.q: What percentage was Sabina's phone at?
qa.a: Nine percent.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she typed the message?
qa.a: She felt hurt and angry, left out of the party.

qa.q: What helped Sabina avoid sending the angry message?
qa.a: Pausing, rereading it and asking herself if she'd still mean it in the morning, then writing a calmer plan.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel if she had received the angry message?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt and defensive, making it harder to sort things out.

grounding: A teenager stops herself from sending an angry message in the heat of the moment the night before an exam.

passage: After the birthday party in Kochi, it was nearly ten, and Jomon, sixteen, stood by the gate with three friends and one scooter. "Triple seat, come on! It's two kilometres," said Arun, already on it. Everyone was laughing, loud, still buzzing from the music. Jomon felt the pull. It would take five minutes. Nobody would know. But he saw the dark road, no streetlights, and remembered his sister Lakshmi's friend who fell off a scooter last year. He stepped back. "I'll call Lakshmi Chechi to pick me up." Arun groaned. "Seriously?" "Seriously." Jomon called. Lakshmi came in ten minutes. In the car he said nothing for a while, then, "They thought I was boring." Lakshmi squeezed his shoulder. "Boring gets home."

qa.q: How far was the ride, according to Arun?
qa.a: Two kilometres.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he felt the pull to get on the scooter?
qa.a: He felt excited and tempted by the fun and the group, but uneasy about the dark road.

qa.q: What helped Jomon make a cooler-headed choice?
qa.a: Pausing to picture the dark road and his sister's friend's fall, and calling Lakshmi instead.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel when Jomon called her?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and proud that he chose safety over pressure.

grounding: A teenager resists peer pressure to ride triple on a scooter at night by calling his sister.

passage:
"Parul, come fast, everyone's jumping off the canal bridge!" Parveen shouted from the gate.
Parul grabbed her slippers. "Wait, how deep is it?"
"Who cares, it's so hot! Everyone's doing it."
Parul's heart was already racing. She could hear the shrieks from the road. Her feet wanted to run.
"Parveen, stop. Did anyone check the water after last week's rain?"
"Stop being boring."
Parul stood still, breathing. "Let's go and look first. If it's too fast, we sit on the bank and eat mangoes. I'm not jumping blind."
At the bridge the water was brown and fast. Two boys were already coughing on the bank. Parul called her uncle, who came and told everyone to get out, and the kids moved to the shallow steps.

qa.q: What was everyone doing at the canal?
qa.a: Jumping off the canal bridge.

qa.q: How did Parul feel when she first heard the shouts?
qa.a: She felt excited and tempted; her heart raced and her feet wanted to run.

qa.q: What helped Parul make a cooler choice?
qa.a: She stopped, breathed and asked about the water, then went to look before deciding, and called her uncle when it was unsafe.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel after seeing the coughing boys?
qa.a: Parveen may feel shaken and relieved that Parul slowed them down.

grounding: Shows a teen pausing under excitement and peer pressure to make a safer decision.

passage:
Last year I almost quit the football team in the middle of a match. I'm Vijay, and I still get hot in the face thinking about it.
The referee gave a penalty against us that I was sure was wrong. Bhupen, our striker, started shouting, and I shouted too. Then I ripped off my captain's armband and threw it on the grass. Everyone stared.
Coach didn't yell. He picked up the band and said, "Sit for five minutes. Then decide."
In those five minutes my breathing slowed. I saw my teammates' faces. I felt ashamed.
I went back on. We lost anyway. But I learned that when I'm boiling, my choices aren't really mine yet. Now I count to ten and look at the sky before I say anything in a match.

qa.q: What did Vijay throw on the grass?
qa.a: The captain's armband.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel after sitting for five minutes?
qa.a: Vijay felt ashamed once the anger cooled and the teammates' faces came into view.

qa.q: What did the coach do that helped?
qa.a: He stayed calm and gave Vijay five minutes before deciding, letting the heat pass before a choice was made.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have seen Vijay's outburst?
qa.a: Bhupen may have felt partly responsible for starting the shouting, and surprised at how far Vijay went.

grounding: A teen recalls a heated decision in a match and learning to wait until the anger cooled.

passage:
Tuition teacher's note on Parul, Class 12
Parul came in on Tuesday furious. Her friend Ritu had told her that a group of girls laughed at her dance video. Parul wanted to post a reply video mocking them, right then.
I asked her to write the post in her notebook instead of her phone and wait until after the maths test. She was annoyed, but agreed.
After the test she read it back and winced. "That's so mean. They'd just screenshot it."
Ritu said the same. Parul tore out the page.
We talked about how anger makes everything feel urgent. She suggested her own rule: nothing gets posted when she's upset, only the next morning. I told her I'd ask about it next week.
She left calmer, still hurt, but in charge of it.

qa.q: What did Parul want to post?
qa.a: A reply video mocking the girls.

qa.q: How did Parul feel when she read the post back after the test?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and uncomfortable, wincing at how mean it sounded.

qa.q: Which step by the teacher helped, and what comes next?
qa.a: The teacher slowed Parul down by having her write it on paper and wait, and plans to check in next week on her own rule.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel about Parul's decision?
qa.a: Ritu may feel relieved, since telling Parul could otherwise have made things worse.

grounding: A teacher records a teen learning to delay a heated choice until she cools down.

passage:
Dear Diary, 11:40 pm
I nearly did something stupid tonight. Nazia posted our group photo from the fest, the one where my eyes are half-shut, and captioned it "sleeping beauty lol". Twenty people reacted. My face burned. I typed a reply about her braces that would have really hurt, and my thumb was literally on send. Then I remembered what happened when Kunal did that last year and the whole class took sides for weeks. I put the phone face down, drank some water, and did ten slow breaths on the balcony. Now it just feels like a silly photo. Tomorrow I'll ask her in person to swap it for a better one. The draft is deleted.
Arohi

qa.q: What did Nazia caption the photo?
qa.a: "sleeping beauty lol"

qa.q: How did Arohi feel when twenty people reacted?
qa.a: Arohi felt humiliated and angry, face burning, wanting to hit back.

qa.q: What helped Arohi step back from sending the reply?
qa.a: Remembering how Kunal's post split the class, then putting the phone down, drinking water and breathing slowly, let the anger cool before deciding.

qa.q: What would change for Nazia if Arohi had sent the reply?
qa.a: Nazia would have been hurt by a comment about her braces, and a small joke could have turned into weeks of taking sides.

grounding: Shows a teenager pausing an angry reply made in the heat of the moment and choosing a calmer response.
